title: Knowledge of Which Presents the Possibility of Exploitation for Personal Gain: Harvard's Own Rule, and the GKO Trade That Broke It
participants: President and Fellows of Harvard College
Nancy Zimmerman / Farallón Fixed Income Associates
U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The sums taken personally were small and that is part of the point: "In July 1996, Hay's father, Dr. Robert Hay, invested $50,000 of Hay's money in Russian government debt instruments known as GKOs. Hay personally made $3,000 from the investment. The investments were made through Zimmerman's company, Farallón Fixed Income Associates." Around December 1995 Hay had also put "some $20,000 in the Flemings Russian Securities Fund managed by Elizabeth Hebert". Three thousand dollars, in a case the United States brought for "substantial damages".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was written into the contract and then disputed from inside. The Regulations Governing Employees barred any employee from engaging "directly or indirectly ... in any business, profession, or occupation in the foreign countries to which the individual is assigned" or making "loans or investments" there. Shleifer, the Project Director, "did not consider himself bound by the policy, however, because it applied to employees and he did not consider himself an employee."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is the court's own subject, and the court names the laundering structure in so many words: "Under Hay's interpretation, however, a grantee employee could 'launder' an investment simply by passing it through one who acts as a broker — even if that broker is the Russia Project's Project Director." On the fund route, the court was equally short: the Flemings fund "as its name implies, invested only in Russian securities", so "Hay's investment in the Fund was plainly an investment in Russian business."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is in the overlap of role and position, and the court documents it with the project's own report to its funder. Hay relied on a manual exemption for government savings certificates that applied only "in those countries in which the work of the project itself or any of its members is unrelated in any way to national financial policies and procedures". The court found: "Hay's work was closely related to national financial policies: Hay admits to involvement in a study of the profits made by broker dealers in the government securities market, and a Legal Reform Project monthly report for USAID stated that during May 1996 the Project, '[t]ogether with the Central Bank and Arthur Andersen consultants,' developed 'the framework for unit investment funds activity on GKO/OFZ ... market.'" Two months later he bought GKOs. Separately, Pallada Asset Management, run by the woman with whom he was involved, "in August 1996, became the sixth company to receive an operating license from the Russian Federal Commission on Securities and the Capital Market" and "In September 1996 ... was the first such company in Russia to register its mutual fund with the Commission."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The outcome split along the institutional line, and the split is the stage. Harvard lost on contract: the Cooperative Agreements "created an obligation to remain free of conflicts of interest", and "actions by Hay and Shleifer breached that duty". But Harvard WON summary judgment on all three False Claims Act counts, because it "did not have knowledge that the claims it submitted were false" and its employees' knowledge could not be imputed since "they were not acting in the scope of employment". All defendants won on common law fraud and fraudulent inducement, because "neither Hay nor Shleifer made false representations to the government" directly — the court noting that under Massachusetts law "[l]iability for common law fraud, unlike the False Claims Act, does not attach where a defendant merely 'causes' a false statement to be made." The individuals carried the fraud findings; the institution carried a contract breach; damages went to a later phase.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Freedom for Russia and the Emerging Eurasian Democracies and Open Market Support Act of 1992, which authorised USAID to help former Soviet states "work toward the creation of democratic institutions and an environment hospitable to foreign investment based upon the rule of law", implemented through a Cooperative Agreement rather than a procurement contract.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A holding that a USAID cooperative agreement is an enforceable contract — the court expressly disagreeing with Trauma Service Group's reasoning that "a cooperative agreement or assistance agreement is not a contract" — which makes conflict-of-interest clauses in aid grants suable in contract. Alongside it, a finding that an institution can escape False Claims Act liability for its employees' conflicts precisely because those employees acted for themselves.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: A project is paid to design a market; designing it means knowing it before anyone else; the knowledge is the thing the conflict rule exists to quarantine; the rule's exemption is read to permit exactly the instrument the project is designing; the investment is routed through the Project Director's spouse's fund; and when it is found out, the institution is liable in contract while the knowledge question defeats the fraud claims against it.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Harvard economists ran Russian privatisation, engineered loans-for-shares to hand the country's assets to a chosen few, and looted Russia on the United States government's payroll.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: THE CASE READ HERE DECIDES NOTHING ABOUT ANY OF THAT, and the dossier will not borrow its authority for claims it does not contain. United States v. President and Fellows of Harvard College is about conflict of interest and false claims under United States law. It contains no finding about loans-for-shares, no finding about Russian privatisation outcomes, no finding about who acquired which Russian asset, and no finding that any Russian state property was transferred to anyone. The word "looting" belongs to the legend, not the judgment. What the judgment does establish is narrower, documented, and in some ways more damning because it is in the defendants' own paperwork. Harvard's own HIID Overseas Manual states the reason for its investment ban, and the reason is this atlas's entire subject: "each HIID overseas group examines under official or semi-official auspices a wide range of local economic matters, knowledge of which at least presents the actual possibility or appearance of exploitation for personal gain." The institution wrote down the hazard, made violation grounds for "immediate dismissal" — and then its Project Director "did not consider himself bound by the policy" because he did not consider himself an employee, while its Moscow General Director, who had helped develop "the framework for unit investment funds activity on GKO/OFZ" market together with the Central Bank, bought GKOs two months later through the Project Director's wife's fund. The court found the contract breached. THE DISPOSITIONS MUST BE REPORTED WHOLE, BECAUSE HALF OF THEM FAVOUR THE DEFENDANTS: Hay lost on two False Claims Act counts and Hay and Shleifer on a third; Harvard won on all three; and all three defendants won on common law fraud and fraudulent inducement. Harvard escaped the fraud counts because it "did not have knowledge" and because its employees "were not acting in the scope of employment" — that is, the institution was cleared on the ground that the men were acting for themselves. Damages were left to a later phase and are not stated here.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: United States v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, Andrei Shleifer, and Jonathan Hay, 323 F. Supp. 2d 151 (D. Mass. 28 June 2004). It records: USAID Cooperative Agreements with the Harvard Institute for International Development in 1992 and effective 11 October 1995 for the "Russia Project", under the 1992 Freedom Support Act; Regulations Governing Employees barring any business or investment in the assigned country, and an HIID Overseas Manual provision barring financial transactions or investments in the Project Country because each overseas group examines local economic matters under official or semi-official auspices, "knowledge of which at least presents the actual possibility or appearance of exploitation for personal gain", with violation grounds for immediate dismissal; Shleifer as Project Director and Principal Investigator, married to Nancy Zimmerman who managed Farallón Fixed Income Associates; Hay as General Director from October 1995, HIID's top adviser in Moscow reporting only to Shleifer, and the Legal Reform Project's principal liaison to USAID; Hay's $20,000 investment around December 1995 in the Flemings Russian Securities Fund managed by Elizabeth Hebert, who ran Pallada Asset Management — licensed sixth by the Russian Federal Commission on Securities and the Capital Market in August 1996 and the first to register a mutual fund with it in September 1996; Hay's $50,000 GKO investment in July 1996 through Zimmerman's firm, returning $3,000, after relying on a manual exemption that applied only where the project's work was unrelated to national financial policies, while a Legal Reform Project monthly report to USAID recorded that in May 1996 the Project had, together with the Central Bank and Arthur Andersen consultants, developed the framework for unit investment funds activity on the GKO/OFZ market; a USAID Inspector General investigation beginning in early 1997, Harvard learning of it in April, suspension of the Project on or about 20 May and by the Russian government the same or next day, Hay's termination on 23 May and Shleifer's removal, and permanent termination on 6 June 1997; suit filed 26 September 2000; and a disposition granting summary judgment against Harvard on breach of contract, against Hay under 31 U.S.C. §§ 3729(a)(1) and (a)(2) and against Hay and Shleifer under § 3729(a)(3), for Harvard on all three False Claims Act counts, and for all defendants on common law fraud and fraudulent inducement, with damages reserved.

citations.title: United States v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, Andrei Shleifer, and Jonathan Hay, 323 F. Supp. 2d 151 (D. Mass., No. CIV.A.00-11977-DPW, 28 June 2004) (Woodlock, J.)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on CourtListener. ACCESS NOTE: courtlistener.com serves search pages to scripted requests but returns an empty HTTP 202 for individual opinion URLs, so this page was opened and read in a browser; link checks may report it blocked. THE CASE: "The United States seeks substantial damages arising from alleged improprieties in a government-sponsored Harvard project to assist Russia in developing capital markets and foreign investments." USAID entered a Cooperative Agreement with the Harvard Institute for International Development in 1992, and a second effective 11 October 1995, under the Freedom for Russia and the Emerging Eurasian Democracies and Open Market Support Act of 1992. THE RULE, AND THE REASON FOR IT IN HARVARD'S OWN WORDS. The Regulations Governing Employees barred any employee from engaging "directly or indirectly ... in any business, profession, or occupation in the foreign countries to which the individual is assigned", or making "loans or investments to or in any business, profession or occupation" there. HIID's own Overseas Manual explained why: "The restriction against any financial transactions or investments in the Project Country arises because each HIID overseas group examines under official or semi-official auspices a wide range of local economic matters, knowledge of which at least presents the actual possibility or appearance of exploitation for personal gain." Violation was grounds for "immediate dismissal". THE POSITIONS HELD: Andrei Shleifer was Project Director throughout, sole Project Director under the second agreement, and also Principal Investigator; an HIID administrator called him the project "Back-stopper", the "responsible senior person in Cambridge". He is married to Nancy Zimmerman, who "managed a hedge fund known as Farallón Fixed Income Associates". Jonathan Hay, a Harvard Law graduate, was the Project's General Director from October 1995, "HIID's top advisor in Moscow", charged with "the overall development, management and implementation of HIID's program", reporting "only to Mr. Shleifer", and the Legal Reform Project's "principal liaison to USAID in Moscow". THE TRANSACTION THAT SHOWS THE MECHANISM MOST PLAINLY: "In July 1996, Hay's father, Dr. Robert Hay, invested $50,000 of Hay's money in Russian government debt instruments known as GKOs. Hay personally made $3,000 from the investment. The investments were made through Zimmerman's company, Farallón Fixed Income Associates." Hay had relied on an Overseas Manual exemption for government savings certificates — but that exemption applied only "in those countries in which the work of the project itself or any of its members is unrelated in any way to national financial policies and procedures", and the court found the opposite: "Hay's work was closely related to national financial policies: Hay admits to involvement in a study of the profits made by broker dealers in the government securities market, and a Legal Reform Project monthly report for USAID stated that during May 1996 the Project, '[t]ogether with the Central Bank and Arthur Andersen consultants,' developed 'the framework for unit investment funds activity on GKO/OFZ (short-term state obligations and federal security bonds) market.'" Also found: Hay invested some $20,000 around December 1995 in the Flemings Russian Securities Fund, managed by Elizabeth Hebert, with whom he was in a relationship and who ran Pallada Asset Management — "in August 1996, became the sixth company to receive an operating license from the Russian Federal Commission on Securities and the Capital Market" and "In September 1996, Pallada was the first such company in Russia to register its mutual fund with the Commission." On the attempt to characterise a transfer through Shleifer as indirect: "Under Hay's interpretation, however, a grantee employee could 'launder' an investment simply by passing it through one who acts as a broker — even if that broker is the Russia Project's Project Director." HOW IT ENDED: USAID's Inspector General began investigating in early 1997; Harvard learned in April 1997; USAID suspended the Project on or about 20 May 1997 and the Russian government did so the same or next day; HIID terminated Hay on 23 May 1997 and removed Shleifer from the Project; USAID terminated it permanently on 6 June 1997. The United States sued on 26 September 2000. THE DISPOSITIONS, WHICH ARE MIXED AND MUST BE STATED AS SUCH: on Count VI (breach of contract) summary judgment was GRANTED against Harvard — the court found "the Cooperative Agreements were valid contracts between Harvard and USAID, that they created an obligation to remain free of conflicts of interest, and that actions by Hay and Shleifer breached that duty". On the False Claims Act counts, judgment was granted against HAY on §§ 3729(a)(1) and (a)(2) and against Hay and Shleifer on § 3729(a)(3); HARVARD WON summary judgment on all three FCA counts, the court finding Harvard "did not have knowledge that the claims it submitted were false" and that Hay's and Shleifer's knowledge could not be imputed because "they were not acting in the scope of employment". On Counts IV (fraud) and VIII (fraudulent inducement) ALL defendants won, because "neither Hay nor Shleifer made false representations to the government" directly and Harvard lacked knowledge. Damages were left to a remedy phase; the court records that the government contended "the conflicts of interest rendered HIID's advice to Russia worthless". WHAT THIS CASE IS NOT ABOUT: it is about conflict of interest and false claims under US law. It contains no finding about loans-for-shares, about Russian privatization outcomes, about who acquired which Russian asset, or about any transfer of Russian state property to anyone. Nothing of that kind is asserted by this dossier from this source.
